title: NASA Announces the X-70, a New Experimental Aircraft
paragraphs: NASA has unveiled the X-70 Fractal, the newest addition to its line of experimental X-planes, at an event at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida on 4 November. The agency describes it as a crewed, high-performance research platform, built to be adaptable so that new aviation technologies can be tested more quickly in real flight.

Published figures include room for up to 2,000 pounds of experimental payloads, carried inside or outside the aircraft and swappable at short notice, a takeoff weight of 10,000 pounds, a cruise speed of Mach 0.75, a ceiling of 45,000 feet and a range of about 1,500 nautical miles. NASA says the aircraft will explore flight-control and manoeuvrability technologies in ways not yet shown in crewed flight, and Laurie Grindle, who directs its aeronautics work, said it was "exciting to bring on another X-plane".

Important details are still missing. The X-70 has not flown, and Administrator Jared Isaacman said only that a first flight under NASA's banner is expected within two years. The release does not name a builder or give a cost, and the images shown are computer-generated rather than photographs of a finished aircraft, so the project's real progress is hard to judge for now.

questions.q: What makes the X-70 designed to be flexible?
questions.a: It carries up to 2,000 pounds of payloads that can be swapped quickly.

questions.q: What is the schedule for the first flight?
questions.a: An expectation of within two years, not a confirmed date.

questions.q: Why is progress hard to judge?
questions.a: The plane has not flown and the images are computer-generated.
